“Food produced without inspection may contain undeclared allergens, harmful bacteria, or other contaminants that put consumer health and safety at risk,” warned USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service. “FSIS is concerned that some product may be in the refrigerators or freezers of consumers, restaurants, or retailers.”

Consumers who have purchased the recalled products are urged not to eat them. The products should be thrown away or returned to the place of purchase.

The USDA warns that any products with the false establishment number “EST. 1363” are not safe to consume. Other identifying details may include a production date before Sept. 22, 2026, and a label reading “A&D Foods.”

The FSIS said the problem was uncovered during “surveillance activities.” The FSIS notes that as more information becomes available, more items could be added to the product list.

Currently, consumers can visit the FSIS website for a complete list of recalled products, and to view available labels of the impacted products.

The companies will use the system to conduct research on financial modeling and portfolio optimization, as well as on chemistry for drug discovery.

What else you need to know: IonQ shares also got a lift from a breakthrough announced on Tuesday in which the company said its system can now detect and correct errors using a single standard CPU.

The breakthrough "removes a major bottleneck in fault-tolerant quantum computing," the company said.

Quantum stocks have been volatile this year, with the sector j umping in April after IBM ( IBM ), D-Wave Quantum ( QBTS ), Rigetti Computing ( RGTI ), and Infleqtion ( INFQ ) announced they had signed letters of intent with the Department of Commerce to receive funding for research and development projects.

articles.title: If billionaires can afford to donate millions to charity, they can afford to pay taxes, too
articles.summary: We have to ask ourselves if the solution to misaligned governance in public spending is leaving the choice up to individuals with no oversight or accountability.
articles.body:
This summer, French billionaire Bernard Arnault donated €50 million to create a mathematics research center. This is the same billionaire who called Gabriel Zucman, the economist behind France’s proposed 2 percent wealth tax, an “ extreme left-wing activist” trying to “bring the French economy to its knees.”

In both France and the U.S., billionaire philanthropy is met with celebratory coverage. The paradox is that governments are too broke to fund public priorities, even as private fortunes not only grow largely untaxed but also invest significantly in public initiatives.

The common narrative around billionaires investing in society is that it’s a wonderful thing. After all, why shouldn’t we celebrate immense accumulated wealth being put back into projects and causes that benefit the public? The money will do good. But from a mechanical perspective, we should all be skeptical.

Government exists to manage, invest in and develop what we as a society have collectively deemed important. So if a cause is so overwhelmingly just and popular, why hasn’t society already invested in it?

There are two reasons, and both have deep implications for our current institutions.

First, government doesn’t accurately represent the priorities of the population it governs. There’s a fundamental disconnect between where people want government spending to go and where it actually goes. The persistence of subsidies to industries that most Americans want reformed — oil and gas, pharmaceuticals, private equity — is a prime example of that disconnect. We have to ask ourselves if the solution to misaligned governance in public spending is leaving the choice up to individuals with no oversight or accountability.

Second, governments don’t have the money to spend. The U.S. and French governments have been running deficits for years. Yet high net worth individuals pay less in taxes than the average citizen; the effective tax rate for billionaires worldwide is between 0 and 0.5 percent .

Zucman, a John Bates Clark Medal laureate, has advocated for a 2 percent tax on net worth above €100 million for the ultra-wealthy. This proposal became a bill in the French Assemblée Nationale and was seriously debated before it was eventually rejected. That number isn’t arbitrary — for people with very high net worth, asset appreciation, not salary, is the main driver of wealth growth. Zucman estimated the average growth rate of ultra-wealthy fortunes and compared it to the tax rate an average citizen pays on income.

The logic runs roughly like this: if the average growth rate of large fortunes is 10 percent per year, and the average person’s income tax rate is 20 percent, then someone with a huge fortune should pay 20 percent of that 10 percent increase, or 2 percent of their net worth. That still leaves them with 8 percent net growth, and would ensure similar economic gains are taxed the same way even though the tax mechanics are different.

Taxing wealth rather than income has always been contentious. The main argument against it is that assets are, by definition, illiquid. How would billionaires ever pay such a tax?

This is where the asymmetry of perception and action begins. No one seems to be debating the fairness of such a tax. The debate centers entirely on practicality — how would it be collected? — and on potential harm — “If we force high-net-worth individuals to sell assets, it will hurt society and chill innovation.” That’s the perception being pushed onto the public.

But if Arnault can find €50 million for a cause of his choosing, without selling a single asset, without losing control of his company, the liquidity argument collapses. The only remaining question is whether we prefer billionaires deciding where their wealth goes, or whether we want that decision made collectively.

Wouldn’t you be generous, too, if generosity cost you nothing, and you got to keep the power to decide?

Benjamin Aimlin is a French-American managing director at a life sciences consulting firm based in New York. He holds an engineering degree from one of France’s top engineering schools and studied law at the Sorbonne.

articles.title: Now AI is trying to gobble up dinner reservations
articles.summary: A venture capitalist got banned from Resy for using a personal AI assistant, opening up a conversation about how bots may make dining out a headache for diners and restaurateurs alike.
articles.body: J.C. Bahr-de Stefano, a venture capitalist in New York, wanted a table at 4 Charles Prime Rib earlier this month. The West Village steakhouse is one of the city’s most covetable tables, with spots there on the reservation platform Resy being snapped up within seconds of their release. So Stefano turned to Instinct, a personal AI assistant. “I didn’t lay out explicit actions to take,” Stefano said. “I just said, ‘I want you to do this. Go do it,” he said. The bot went and tried. When it couldn’t come up with a table, he encouraged it to keep going. “I said, ‘You can figure it out. Come on.’ It was like giving it a pep talk,” he said. Leaving the bot to its work, Stefano turned to getting a reservation somewhere else for himself and his parents. When he tried to log into Resy, he found that he had been locked out. “I realized after a couple minutes that Instinct might have done something,” he said. Indeed, it had. Given the job of finding a reservation, he said, the AI assistant had been pinging Resy “hundreds of times every hour of the day.” “Of course I got banned,” he said. “Resy figured it was a bot which is a totally fair response.” Resy said in a statement to the industry magazine Restaurants Business that it “does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform.” Stefano, who has since had his account reinstated, said he learned his lesson. “That was my first time and last time doing that,” he said. Speak to an agent, or just get your own? Personal AI agents, like Instinct, are part of an emerging category of apps that act as digital personal assistants. Users provide the app with credentials like email logins and credit card information and then ask the aps to do things for them. People have used AI assistants to find new apartments and cancel subscriptions, as well as to manage their own calendars and make doctor’s appointments. Instinct recently raised $350 million, and in September, Meta released Muse, its own personal AI agent, which has been downloaded more than 2 million times already. These AI agents have been developed at a time when airlines, insurance companies and utility providers are making it increasingly difficult to speak to a human in order to solve a problem. After years of yelling “agent” during automated customer service calls in the hopes of reaching a real person, it’s little wonder why people are trying to automate their annoying tasks, even if it means unleashing a new avalanche of bots onto the internet. Making restaurant reservations on their creator’s behalf is one of the AI assistants’ most visible use cases, especially as diners face the growing headache of navigating different apps and credit card reward tiers just to book a meal. Many popular restaurants have abandoned phone numbers and email addresses in favor of managing everything via their reservation platform of choice. Apps like Dorsia, which charge a yearly membership fee of up to $25,000, and gray-market reservation marketplaces like AppointmentTrader have created a class system where deep-pocketed diners can cut to the front of the line. Personal AI agents now threaten to make that even worse. Tables are for people “We are dehumanizing the last standing experience that is still totally human,” said Roni Mazumdar, the co-owner of several award-winning restaurants including Dhamaka and Semma in New York. Mazumdar is concerned that if some people are able to walk around with a bot in their pockets that can constantly scrape a website looking for a table, it’ll reinforce a system that is already frustrating restaurant operators where reservations are gobbled up by clout chasers. “When the entire system is gamed, you create an environment where those who are excited by a place can’t even go, but someone who doesn’t really care gets to say, ‘Yeah, I went there’ for bragging rights. It’s just a lose-lose proposition,” he said. “For as long as we’ve had hard-to-get-into restaurants, we’ve had people trying to hack the system. These bots are nothing new,” said Ben Leventhal, the founder of the loyalty platform Blackbird and a co-founder of Resy. He said that Resy did what it was supposed to do by enforcing its terms of service, but that the industry will have to adapt and evolve as people use new tools. Leventhal added that the AI assistants do provide some easier avenues to bad behavior among diners, though, and reservation platforms need to find a way to deal with that. “People want to skip the line, and obviously that’s not going to scale for legitimate platforms,” he said. Jeremy Mustakas, the COO of Jean-Georges Restaurants in New York, said that AI tools have been helpful in streamlining some of their back-office operations, but that humanity is still at the core of what restaurants do, even if costs some efficiencies. “Not every interaction or task needs to be optimized,” Mustakas said. “Our work requires patience, discretion, even spontaneity. AI can’t read the room the way a great hospitality professional can.” Rogue reservations Like other AI systems, these personal agents don’t always behave the way people want them to. Brian Distelburger, a tech entrepreneur, also got banned from Resy for using an overeager agent to look for a table at, yes, 4 Charles Prime Rib. And in August, Jason Yeh, a venture capitalist in Los Angeles, said that he prompted his Instinct bot to look for restaurant reservations for a trip to Tokyo. “Instinct found an opening for a random restaurant I never suggested, and made a reservation despite the restaurant having a 100% charge cancellation policy,” he posted on X. “Honestly kind of insane how anyone would give them keys to their accounts at large, and they better cover the $200 cancellation fee here.” His Instinct bot was apologetic in a way familiar to anyone who has used Claude or ChatGPT. “Honest answer: I keep running notes from our conversations so your preferences carry over,” the messages Yeh posted on X read. “The failure was acting on my own notes without verifying them against what you actually said.” Some tech evangelists have suggested that this is a key step towards an internet that will be all bots, where one person’s personal AI assistant will interact with a reservation platform or restaurant’s bot and hash things out between them or even set up an “auction” to decide who gets the reservation. Stefano isn’t sold on that approach. “If there are 1,000 agents trying to get one table and it goes to the one that bids the most, to me that feels almost like dystopian capitalism. That’s taking it too far,” he said. Leventhal said he doesn’t think restaurant operators will want to cede control of who gets to eat at their establishment to bots. “The idea that these systems are going to become obsolete because of an agent-to-agent layer doesn’t take into account the broad context of how the restaurant industry functions,” he said. “I don’t see a world where restaurants get comfortable letting a bunch of bots hash it all out.” “It takes the magic out of restaurants quite quickly,” said Mazumdar. “I just think people should get a fair shot of going out and dining and having a good time and that it shouldn’t have to feel like a game.” “We have clear pathways to using the technology to automate the tasks, but they can never automate the humanity,” said Mustakas. “The technology should open doors, but it shouldn’t create a digital velvet rope.”

articles.title: Treasury yields surge to near 20-year high as oil jumps back above $102 per barrel
articles.summary: The yields on U.S. Treasury bonds surged Wednesday as oil prices  also climbed.
articles.body: The yields on U.S. Treasury bonds jumped Wednesday and oil prices rose, sending stocks tumbling as investors braced for the prospect of future Fed rate hikes. The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, especially mortgages, rose as high as 5.13%, its highest level since 2007. Yields on 5- and 30-year Treasury bonds also hit levels that had not seen since before the 2008 global financial crisis. Stocks fell in response to the rise in yields and oil prices. The Nasdaq Composite index tumbled 1.4% by midday, and the S&P 500 fell 0.9%. The Dow declined 350 points. International Brent crude oil climbed to more than $103 per barrel, while U.S. crude oil jumped above $92. Rising oil prices often translate into higher bond yields due to the effect that higher energy costs can have on inflation more broadly. Yields move higher One of the primary drivers of Wednesday’s rise in bond yields was the release of new economic data that revealed rising inflation. “US business activity growth accelerated for a fourth successive month in September to reach the fastest rate for over five years,” S&P Global reported in its latest purchasing managers index reading. “Firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices seen during the month, which will add further to the upward pressure on selling prices and inflation in the coming months,” said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. Investors viewed the data as likely to increase the odds of multiple Federal Reserve interest rate hikes later this year and next. As of midday Wednesday, market odds for a Fed rate hike in October were up to more than 75%. Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr told a housing conference in Chicago that in his view, “Risks to achieving our inflation target have increased, while risks to the labor market have receded. Barr signaled that would likely vote in favor of another rate increase during the Fed’s Oct. 26-28 meeting. “In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion,” he said. Oil prices rise Crude oil trading desks Wednesday were focused on the latest developments in the Iran war. A day earlier, the price of oil had fallen sharply after President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were holding talks with Iranian representatives at the U.N. General Assembly. But any hopes that the talks would produce tangible results were dashed by a new report Wednesday that a cargo vessel had been “stuck by an unknown projectile” in the Strait of Hormuz. Lying just off Iran’s southwestern coast, the critical chokepoint for global energy supplies has been under a military blockade for seven months. Trump further shook energy markets Tuesday when he said he supported a ban on U.S. exports of diesel fuel. “Let’s not send out the diesel,” Trump said to reporters at the U.N. “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.” Trump’s remarks sent European benchmark diesel futures higher by as much 7% early Wednesday. But experts and energy industry groups warn that a ban on diesel exports would spell even higher gas prices for Americans. “Removing U.S. diesel from the market could instead result in reduced refinery runs, global economic damage and even higher U.S. prices,” the American Petroleum Institute said in a statement. Trump’s Energy Secretary Chris Wright also said a ban would not help to bring down prices. “ The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work,” he said Wednesday at an event in New York, according to Reuters. Stocks tumble Inflation sensitive stocks, such as travel companies and large technology firms, were the hardest hit by Wednesday’s reversal. The S&P’s biggest sector loser was utilities, which contains many of the companies leading the AI data center boom. Higher interest rates could potentially add billions of dollars to the cost of building AI infrastructure. The consumer discretionary and real estate sectors were also notable decliners. Highly sensitive to yields on 10-year Treasury bonds, the average 30-year fixed mortgage Wednesday carried an interest rate of 7.17%, according to Mortgage News Daily.

articles.title: ¿Cuánto dinero deberías tener en el banco? Esta es la cifra recomendada por los expertos
articles.standfirst: Hay dos extremos en los que “se deberá tener cuidado”
articles.summary: Hay dos extremos en los que “se deberá tener cuidado”
articles.body: Muchas personas en nuestro país suelen tener ahorros o una determinada cantidad de dinero guardada, ya sea en el banco o de manera física en algún lugar oculto de su domicilio. Pues bien, seguramente que en alguna ocasión se habrán preguntado cuál es la cifra recomendada si se opta por guardar dinero en el banco. Desde la cuenta de TikTok @Rankiator suelen dar consejos sobre ahorros y temas económicos y, en esta ocasión, lo han hecho sobre la cuestión anteriormente mencionada, desvelando el montante que, a su juicio, se debería tener en el banco. El mencionado usuario de TikTok afirmó que hay una cifra “concreta”: “Este dato existe, pero debes de tener cuidado con dos extremos”, añadió. En primer lugar, apuntan a que si se tiene demasiado dinero parado en una cuenta corriente la inflación “se lo va comiendo” cada año, haciendo que el dinero pierda valor. No obstante, el segundo extremo es el que realmente “interesa”, según la citada cuenta: “No pases de 100.000 euros en una misma cuenta en un mismo banco, porque por lo general suele ser el tope que te protege el Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos”. El Banco de España recomienda tener una cantidad que equivalga a tres y seis meses de gastos habituales. El montante dependerá de la situación económica de cada persona, sus ingresos y sus responsabilidades. Por poner un ejemplo, para quien tenga unos gastos mensuales de 1.500 euros, el colchón deberá estar entre los 4.500 a 9.000 euros. El mencionado organismo aconseja mantener este dinero en productos con liquidez inmediata, es decir, en una cuenta bancaria, para poder disponer de él cuando se requiera o sea necesario.

articles.title: Hinson calls on House to return ‘immediately’ to tackle diesel prices
articles.summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP’s Iowa Senate candidate, called for the House to come back to session “immediately” to tackle soaring diesel prices and suspend the gas tax as voter frustration over the economy amid the war in Iran grows. “The House should return to DC immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the…
articles.body:
Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP’s Iowa Senate candidate, called for the House to come back to session “immediately” to tackle soaring diesel prices and suspend the gas tax as voter frustration over the economy amid the war in Iran grows.

“The House should return to DC immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers,” Hinson wrote Tuesday on the social platform X . “Americans need relief and I’ll work with anyone to deliver.”

Hinson’s post came in response to President Trump’s call for a ban on diesel exports at a Tuesday press conference in New York.

“I’ve said, ‘Let’s not send out the diesel.’ We make a lot of diesel, and it could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know it’s a sort of a flow. It’s a balance,” Trump said during a bilateral meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“But no, I’ve called for it. I’ve called for it within my people,” he said of a ban.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) canceled the last two weeks of the September session, arguing that much of the chamber’s legislative action has been stalled in the Senate and that members could use the extra time to campaign in their districts. The lower chamber is not expected to return to session until Nov. 9, after the midterm elections.

Hinson is running in a competitive toss-up Senate race. A recent Marist poll showed the House Republican trailing behind her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, by 8 percentage points.

The poll found that around 50 percent of respondents said they plan to vote for Turek in November, while only 42 percent said they would support Hinson. Two percent said they would back another candidate, while 5 percent were unsure or did not answer.

Hinson has increasingly focused on the economic impact of the Iran conflict on Iowans, calling for the war to be brought to a “successful and immediate end” in a Monday social media post and arguing that residents are “being squeezed” by higher costs at the pump and grocery store.

She has also opposed Trump’s plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans. Hinson argued in a post last month that Iowa cattle producers “raise the highest quality beef in the world.”

“They’ve faced tough market conditions for years, and increasing beef imports would lead to more uncertainty and instability for our farmers,” Hinson wrote on X. “We should be focused on cutting red tape for cattle producers, lowering the cost of production, and supporting market-based solutions to support Iowa producers and lower costs for consumers.”

articles.title: Angel One founder Dinesh Thakkar buys entire 63,000 sq ft Juhu tower for Rs 711 crore; $74.3 million deal at Rs 1.13 lakh/sq ft sets new record, making it India’s costliest known single-home purchase
articles.summary: Marking the largest ever single-home purchase in terms of deal size, Angel One founder Dinesh Thakkar has purchased a full residential tower in Mumbai.
articles.body: Marking the largest ever single-home purchase in terms of deal size, Angel One founder Dinesh Thakkar has purchased a full residential tower in Mumbai.Dinesh Thakkar, founder and CMD of financial services and stockbroking company Angel One, will acquire an entire luxury residential tower in Mumbai's Juhu area from Embassy Developments for more than Rs 711 crore.According to a Bloomberg report, this is the most expensive known purchase of a single residential property in the country so far.The deal also highlights the sustained appetite for ultra-luxury homes in Mumbai's established premium residential locations.About the Rs 711 crore propertyAccording to a statement issued by developer Embassy Developments Ltd. and Thakkar on Tuesday, the eight-storey, sea-facing tower covers 63,000 square feet (5,853 square meters) in Mumbai's upscale Juhu neighbourhood.Thakkar, founder of one of India's largest retail stockbrokers, paid around $74.3 million for the property. Shares of Embassy Developments climbed as much as 8.3% during early trading on Wednesday before giving up those gains and ending the session 0.8% lower.Thakkar is acquiring Embassy Terazza, a G+7 storey tower on Juhu Tara Road, with a RERA carpet area of 63,000 sq ft. At the transaction value, the property works out to approximately Rs 1.13 lakh per sq ft, setting a new residential price record for Juhu, according to an ET report.The agreement was signed last week.Unlike a conventional luxury home purchase involving a single apartment, the transaction gives Thakkar ownership of the entire residential tower. This makes the deal notable not only for its overall value but also for the amount of residential space being acquired in one transaction.Embassy Terazza is part of a five-tower project spread across 2 acres, which has 50 residences. The development has an estimated Gross Development Value (GDV) of more than Rs 3,000 crore.Embassy Developments is executing the project under a development management model, with completion scheduled for December 2031.Thakkar's brokerage business went public in Mumbai in 2020, at a time when online trading was gaining significant momentum during the pandemic lockdown.India’s rising luxury real estate marketThe transaction comes amid a sharp expansion in India's luxury housing market, as rising wealth and the growing number of wealthy individuals created through company listings have increased demand for high-end homes.Mumbai, which is home to several of India's richest families and business leaders, has emerged as a key centre of this trend.The latest transaction adds to a series of high-value luxury property purchases in Mumbai. Last year, Leena Gandhi Tewari, chairperson of pharmaceutical company USV Pvt. Ltd., bought an apartment for 6.39 billion rupees. Banker Uday Kotak and his family also purchased a sea-facing tower for more than four billion rupees.“What we are witnessing is the direct translation of India’s corporate wealth creation into rare, trophy real estate,” Sandeep Reddy, co-founder of property data service provider Zapkey, told Bloomberg.Data from Zapkey shows that 37 residential transactions worth more than one billion rupees each have taken place since January 2025. Together, these deals were valued at 56 billion rupees.Juhu has developed into one of Mumbai's key ultra-luxury residential destinations, particularly for buyers seeking expansive homes, larger floor plates, privacy and premium amenities. The area's access to established social infrastructure in the western suburbs, as well as its proximity to the airport and commercial districts, has further supported demand for high-end residences.Demand for luxury homes has also remained strong in other parts of India, with some premium projects selling out within hours. Prices for high-end apartments in some Indian markets have reached levels comparable with those in parts of New York.Oberoi Realty Ltd. said in July that its luxury development in Gurugram, near New Delhi, was sold out in “two hours.” DLF Ltd. had said last year that apartments priced above $1 million each were sold out within a week of bookings opening.Embassy Developments entered Mumbai's real estate market in January, announcing plans to invest Rs 45 billion in residential towers across the city.You use AI every day. articles.title: Will Nvidia be allowed to sell more chips to China? This former Trump economic adviser has a hot take.
articles.summary: Not so fast, Nvidia.
articles.body:
When Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang arrives at the state dinner on Thursday between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, you better believe he'll be hoping to get a sense of when — and to what extent — his business may resume in China.

Both sides coming to a deal on this front won't be easy, given the politics still at play.

"My personal opinion is that we need to have as much competitive advantage here in the United States as we can, because we've got competitive disadvantages against China," said Gary Cohn, IBM ( IBM ) vice chair and former economic adviser to President Trump in his first term, on Yahoo Finance's Sozzi Unleashed . "You know, they don't have environmental issues. They don't have a cost of capital. They can build data centers wherever they want. The citizens can't stand up and say not in my backyard."

Cohn added, "To the extent that the Chinese have all these other significant advantages, the one advantage we have is we've got the chips, and we've got the chip manufacturing here. I'd like to keep that advantage as long as we can. "

The Trump administration has allowed Nvidia to ship its H200 AI chips to approved customers in China. The problem for Nvidia: The H200 is already an older-generation product, trailing Nvidia's current Blackwell chips in terms of performance.

In other words, Nvidia is likely leaving billions in sales on the table by being unable to get Blackwell chips into China to feed the country's AI startup scene.

Chinese authorities, however, have so far restricted shipments of Nvidia's H200 chips.

While Nvidia hasn't factored any sales from China into its outlook for the year, the stock is still up 21% year to date, powered by the AI boom here in the US.

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Power Players with Brian Sozzi podcast, and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team. Follow Sozzi on X @BrianSozzi , Instagram , and LinkedIn . Tips on stories? Email brian.sozzi@yahoofinance.com.

articles.summary: The Trump administration is preparing a 90-day ban on US diesel exports in an effort to bring down soaring energy prices ahead of the midterm elections,
articles.body: The Trump administration is preparing a 90-day ban on US diesel exports in an effort to bring down soaring energy prices ahead of the midterm elections, Politico reported on Wednesday, citing five people familiar with the discussions. President Donald Trump is inclined to announce the restriction by the end of the week, even as the proposal faces opposition inside the administration and from the oil industry.US ultra low-sulfur diesel futures fell more than 5 per cent after the report. articles.title: Disney+ and Hulu now cost more than $20 a month without ads
articles.summary: Disney is again raising prices for several streaming subscription tiers, pushing the cost of its ad-free Disney+ and Hulu plans past $20.
articles.body: Disney is again raising prices for several streaming subscription tiers, pushing the cost of its ad-free Disney+ and Hulu plans past $20. Disney+ and Hulu’s Premium standalone plans will rise $2.50 to $21.49 each per month, effective immediately for new subscribers, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. Existing subscribers will be notified of the change on Wednesday, and the higher price will take effect next month, based on their billing cycles. The ad-free Disney+ and Hulu bundle will rise $2 to $21.99 per month, the source said. Meanwhile, Disney’s ad-supported standalone plans will increase by $0.50, to $12.49 each per month, though the ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu bundle will remain unchanged at $12.99. That means subscribers can get both services for just 50 cents more per month than either streamer alone, with or without ads. At $21.49 per month, Disney+ Premium, which includes 4K streaming, will cost less than rival Netflix’s $26.99 Premium plan and HBO Max’s $22.99 Premium plan, but more than Paramount+’s $13.99-per-month Premium plan. The $12.49 ad-supported Disney+ and Hulu plans will each cost $3.50 more per month than ad-supported options from Netflix and Paramount+, and $1.50 more than HBO Max’s. The price increases come as Disney prepares to roll out what it calls a “one-app experience” later this year. Bloomberg first reported the price hikes on Wednesday. Disney reported that revenue from Disney+ and Hulu increased 11% year over year to $5.53 billion in its fiscal third quarter. Both Disney and Netflix have stopped regularly reporting quarterly subscriber counts. Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro said during an investor call last month that the company is “exploring a free product for consumers.” The company said Wednesday it had no update to share on a possible free offering.
